title: The Veterans Affairs suicide-risk model REACH VET is associated with fewer documented suicide attempts, admissions and emergency visits among veterans in the top 0.1% risk tier, with no change in deaths
summary: A study by the Veterans Affairs office that runs REACH VET found that veterans flagged by its suicide-risk model had fewer suicide attempts and admissions and no change in deaths.
account: The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) announced REACH VET (Recovery Engagement and Coordination for Health - Veterans Enhanced Treatment) on 3 April 2017. It had begun as a pilot the previous October and was fully implemented across VA. It uses a predictive model on veterans' health records to identify those at statistically elevated risk of suicide and other adverse outcomes. Once a veteran is identified, a VA mental health or primary care provider reaches out. The provider reviews the condition and treatment plan and decides whether enhanced care is needed. Nextgov/FCW (17 July 2025) says that the model scans records monthly for the top 0.1% risk tier. It says that the variable set was cut from 381 to 61 and that about 30,000 veterans were identified in the first year. Nextgov (18 October 2024) gives about 6,700 veterans a month. McCarthy and colleagues published the evaluation in JAMA Network Open on 18 October 2021. They are at the VA Office of Mental Health and Suicide Prevention, which built and runs the program. It covered 173,313 individuals, 40,816 of them in the top 0.1% tier during REACH VET (March 2017 to December 2018). The pre-period (March 2014 to December 2015) had 36,604. Triple-difference analyses found that REACH VET was associated with more completed outpatient appointments (adjusted triple difference 0.31; 95% confidence interval 0.06 to 0.55). The proportion with new safety plans rose (0.08; 0.06 to 0.10). Mental health admissions (-0.08; -0.10 to -0.05), emergency department visits (-0.03; -0.06 to -0.01) and documented suicide attempts (-0.05; -0.06 to -0.03) fell. Subcohort analyses found no difference in suicide or all-cause mortality. Care evaluations of identified veterans rose from 46.1% to 87.5% over the period. A 2022 Psychiatric Services paper reports that by October 2020, 98% of identified veterans (N=6,579) were contacted and had care evaluated. On 30 May 2024 The Fuller Project, in a story copublished by The Markup, reported from VA documents and interviews that the model favors men and that officials left military sexual trauma out of its 61 variables. Matthew Miller, VA's executive director for suicide prevention, told the reporter that officials excluded it because it was not among the strongest predictors of suicide risk. Nextgov (2024) reports that research found that the model “considered being a white man more of an indicator of potential self-harm than other factors”. Nextgov reports that a REACH VET 2.0 adding military sexual trauma and intimate partner violence as risk factors was planned for early 2025. Dent, Cooper and McCarthy (JAMA Network Open, 8 July 2025; 266,246 observations) again found no association with suicide, external-cause or all-cause mortality. The 6-month suicide hazard ratio was 1.18 (95% confidence interval 0.83–1.69). The program's benefit is a cohort-level association over 2017–2018, with no single dated event.
purpose: Built to identify veterans in the top 0.1% of predicted suicide risk each month so that clinicians re-evaluate and enhance their care. The measured associations are that purpose.
system: REACH VET (Recovery Engagement and Coordination for Health - Veterans Enhanced Treatment) suicide-risk predictive model and care-enhancement program
model_version: Original 2017 model (381 variables reduced to 61, per Nextgov); REACH VET 2.0 announced for 2025
developer: US Department of Veterans Affairs, Office of Mental Health and Suicide Prevention
segment: Health-system predictive risk modeling and outreach
taxonomy_note: The outcomes are mental-health care results (fewer attempts, admissions and ED visits) with no effect on deaths, from a VA-authored cohort study.

ratings.reason: The 2021 study reports changes for cohorts of veterans. No individual veteran's outcome is documented, and mortality did not differ in 2021 or 2025.

VA-authored papers report measurable gains in care. Completed outpatient visits and new safety plans rose for identified veterans, and care evaluations rose from 46.1% to 87.5% of them between March 2017 and December 2018.

The VA-authored evaluation reports fewer documented suicide attempts, mental health admissions and emergency visits across 40,816 top-risk veterans. It found no change in suicide or all-cause deaths, so no lives saved are documented.

ai_role.statement: The predictive model selects the monthly top 0.1% risk tier. Coordinators and providers then re-evaluate care and reach out, so the clinical response, not the model alone, produces any change. The evaluation is observational, uses a triple-difference design to handle non-parallel trends, and is authored by the VA office that built and runs REACH VET. It found no mortality association, replicated in 2025 by the same group. Independent reporting documents that the original model weighted being a white man heavily and omitted military sexual trauma.

fields.account: The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) announced REACH VET (Recovery Engagement and Coordination for Health - Veterans Enhanced Treatment) on 3 April 2017. It had begun as a pilot the previous October and was fully implemented across VA. It uses a predictive model on veterans' health records to identify those at statistically elevated risk of suicide and other adverse outcomes. Once a veteran is identified, a VA mental health or primary care provider reaches out. The provider reviews the condition and treatment plan and decides whether enhanced care is needed. Nextgov/FCW (17 July 2025) says that the model scans records monthly for the top 0.1% risk tier. It says that the variable set was cut from 381 to 61 and that about 30,000 veterans were identified in the first year. Nextgov (18 October 2024) gives about 6,700 veterans a month. McCarthy and colleagues published the evaluation in JAMA Network Open on 18 October 2021. They are at the VA Office of Mental Health and Suicide Prevention, which built and runs the program. It covered 173,313 individuals, 40,816 of them in the top 0.1% tier during REACH VET (March 2017 to December 2018). The pre-period (March 2014 to December 2015) had 36,604. Triple-difference analyses found that REACH VET was associated with more completed outpatient appointments (adjusted triple difference 0.31; 95% confidence interval 0.06 to 0.55). The proportion with new safety plans rose (0.08; 0.06 to 0.10). Mental health admissions (-0.08; -0.10 to -0.05), emergency department visits (-0.03; -0.06 to -0.01) and documented suicide attempts (-0.05; -0.06 to -0.03) fell. Subcohort analyses found no difference in suicide or all-cause mortality. Care evaluations of identified veterans rose from 46.1% to 87.5% over the period. A 2022 Psychiatric Services paper reports that by October 2020, 98% of identified veterans (N=6,579) were contacted and had care evaluated. On 30 May 2024 The Fuller Project, in a story copublished by The Markup, reported from VA documents and interviews that the model favors men and that officials left military sexual trauma out of its 61 variables. Matthew Miller, VA's executive director for suicide prevention, told the reporter that officials excluded it because it was not among the strongest predictors of suicide risk. Nextgov (2024) reports that research found that the model “considered being a white man more of an indicator of potential self-harm than other factors”. Nextgov reports that a REACH VET 2.0 adding military sexual trauma and intimate partner violence as risk factors was planned for early 2025. Dent, Cooper and McCarthy (JAMA Network Open, 8 July 2025; 266,246 observations) again found no association with suicide, external-cause or all-cause mortality. The 6-month suicide hazard ratio was 1.18 (95% confidence interval 0.83–1.69). The program's benefit is a cohort-level association over 2017–2018, with no single dated event.

fields.headline: REACH VET flags veterans who then attempt suicide less; deaths unchanged

provenance.basis: REACH VET prompted clinician outreach for a risk-ranked group. The later mortality study found no statistically detectable mortality reduction through 24 months. A VA spokesperson described planned model revisions. The mortality confidence intervals permit benefits or harms. The reported model revision was a plan, not confirmation of deployment. Original effectiveness study: Methods; mortality follow-up: Methods and Results; October 2024 Nextgov interview with VA.
